angle_gap: The piece frames skills-based hiring as 'gaining ground... with mixed results' but (per its title/dek, the only readable content — the body is CMS wreckage) stops at reporting adoption trends and mixed outcomes; it never explains WHY some programs get mixed results while others succeed, i.e. no breakdown of the assessment-design practices (validated skills tests vs. a resume-blind policy with no real test behind it) that separate the wins from the failures.
asset: Why Skills-Based Hiring Gets Mixed Results — And What the Successful Programs Do Differently
distinct_angle: Goes past the trend-adoption stats to the practical dividing line the SHRM piece never draws: employers who pair the skills-based pledge with a validated assessment see the gains, those who just drop the degree requirement see the 'mixed results' — a distinction a writer can build from public case studies and existing research on skills-based hiring outcomes.

angle_gap: The article covers Title III website-accessibility litigation for general public-facing business sites in depth (lawsuit counts, DOJ guidance, poor-color-contrast/no-alt-text checklist) but only gestures at the employment side — it cuts off mid-sentence on 'ADA Requires Help for Employees, Too' (Title I) and never addresses accessibility inside a hiring or testing workflow specifically, e.g. accessible online job applications or pre-employment assessments for candidates with disabilities.
asset: Making Pre-Employment Tests ADA-Compliant: What the DOJ's Accessibility Guidance Means for Hiring Assessments
distinct_angle: Where the source page stays at the general Title III public-accommodations level and drops the Title I employment thread unfinished, ours follows that thread through to the end — applying the DOJ's own accessibility criteria (color contrast, alt-text, keyboard navigation, accessible forms) specifically to online job applications and skills assessments, the exact gap the original leaves open.
